name: Washington, D.C.
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Washington, D.C.: government contractor due diligence, False Claims Act support and federal disputes.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters that run through Washington, D.C.: federal and District government contractors, False Claims Act and whistleblower matters, litigation in the federal and local courts, trade associations, international organisations and policy-facing businesses. Scoped from Nashville, with licensed local investigators where fieldwork is needed.
intro: Washington, D.C. is the seat of the United States federal government and a city whose economy is built around it. The District had an estimated 693,645 residents in July 2025, at the centre of a metropolitan region that extends into Maryland and Virginia. Federal departments and agencies, Congress, the federal courts, government contractors, law and lobbying firms, consultancies, trade and professional associations, think tanks, media organisations and international institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund give the city a concentration of policy, regulatory and procurement activity found nowhere else in the country.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Washington because government money, regulation and influence meet there. Common triggers include due diligence on federal and District contractors, subcontractors and teaming partners; support to counsel in False Claims Act matters, whether brought by the Department of Justice and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia or under the District's own False Claims Act; background research on proposed board members, executives and advisers with government or political histories; and inquiries into grant fraud, procurement irregularities, conflicts of interest and undisclosed foreign ties. Litigation in the federal and local courts in the city also generates demand for witness location and party background research.

matters.title: Government contractor due diligence
matters.text: Ownership, management, litigation and performance research on federal and District contractors, subcontractors and teaming partners, including size and status representations, affiliations, past debarment or suspension and False Claims Act history, for acquirers, primes and investors assessing procurement and reputational exposure.

matters.title: False Claims Act matter support
matters.text: Fact development, chronology work and background research on relators, witnesses and counterparties in federal or District False Claims Act matters, supporting defence counsel or relators' counsel, with findings structured so counsel can assess them against the statutory elements and the record.

matters.title: Political and regulatory background research
matters.text: Lawful research on proposed directors, executives, advisers and lobbying counterparts with government or political histories, covering public disclosures, litigation, prior roles, business affiliations and media, to inform appointments, partnerships and reputational risk decisions in a city where these histories matter.

matters.title: Foreign influence and ownership reviews
matters.text: Research into undisclosed foreign ownership, funding or control behind contractors, associations, consultancies and investment vehicles operating in Washington, drawing on corporate records, public filings and open sources across jurisdictions, to support compliance reviews, transaction diligence and counsel's assessment of disclosure obligations.

matters.title: Grant and nonprofit integrity inquiries
matters.text: Inquiries into misuse of grant funds, related-party transactions and governance failures at Washington-based nonprofits, associations and grant recipients, combining public filings, corporate records and interviews arranged with counsel, for boards, funders, auditors and the counsel advising them on disclosure and recovery.

local_context.title: Federal courts in Washington
local_context.text: The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit sit in the city and hear a large share of cases involving federal agencies, regulatory challenges and government contracts. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia participates in federal False Claims Act enforcement; in 2016, for example, the United States filed a False Claims Act suit in the District Court over inflated claims under a State Department contract.

local_context.title: District False Claims Act
local_context.text: The District has its own False Claims Act, D.C. Code sections 2-381.01 to 2-381.09, enforced by the Office of the Attorney General for the District of Columbia. It targets false claims to obtain or keep District funds, such as payment for work not fully or properly performed, and many recoveries involve Medicaid fraud. The Act provides for treble damages, civil penalties and qui tam actions, alongside protections for whistleblowers.

local_context.title: Private detective licensing in D.C.
local_context.text: The District licenses private detectives and private detective agencies through the Security Officers Management Branch of the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection. Licensing information published by a compliance service indicates surety bond requirements of 25,000 dollars for agencies and 5,000 dollars for individual detectives, with renewals in even-numbered years. Fieldwork in the District is carried out only by appropriately licensed investigators.

local_context.title: D.C. Superior Court and local records
local_context.text: The Superior Court of the District of Columbia is the local trial court for civil, criminal, probate and landlord-tenant matters, with appeals to the D.C. Court of Appeals. Business entity records are maintained by DLCP's corporations function, and real property records by the District's Recorder of Deeds. Together with federal court dockets, these are core sources for background research on Washington parties.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Washington, TDSC first separates the federal and District dimensions: a contractor issue may involve federal procurement rules, the federal False Claims Act and the D.C. federal courts, or District contracts, the District False Claims Act and the Superior Court. Research relies on federal and local court dockets, entity and property records, procurement and award data, lobbying and other public disclosures, and open sources. TDSC does not use pretexting or access restricted government systems. Where surveillance, interviews or other fieldwork in the District is needed, TDSC coordinates investigators licensed by DLCP and works with the client's counsel. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office in Washington.

faqs.q: Do private investigators need a licence in Washington, D.C.?
faqs.a: Yes. The District licenses private detectives and private detective agencies through the Security Officers Management Branch of the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection, with bonding requirements. When a TDSC matter requires fieldwork in the District, it is carried out by investigators holding the appropriate D.C. licence, coordinated within an agreed written scope.

faqs.q: Can TDSC support a False Claims Act case in Washington?
faqs.a: Yes, as a consultant to counsel for either side. TDSC develops chronologies, researches parties, witnesses and corporate relationships, and analyses public procurement and court records. Whether a matter falls under the federal Act or the District's False Claims Act, legal strategy and filings remain with counsel.

faqs.q: Does the District have its own False Claims Act?
faqs.a: Yes. The District of Columbia False Claims Act, D.C. Code sections 2-381.01 to 2-381.09, is enforced by the D.C. Office of the Attorney General and covers false claims to obtain or keep District funds. It allows treble damages, civil penalties and qui tam actions, and it protects whistleblowers.

faqs.q: How does TDSC research a government contractor?
faqs.a: TDSC combines entity records, federal and local court dockets, award and procurement data, exclusion and debarment information, ownership and affiliation research, and media review. The aim is to identify undisclosed relationships, litigation and enforcement history, and representations that may not hold up, without any access to non-public government systems.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Washington, D.C.?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville, Tennessee, and has no office, staff or address in Washington. Engagements touching the District are scoped and managed from Nashville, with D.C.-licensed investigators coordinated for any local fieldwork and the client's counsel directing legal aspects. Fieldwork is never undertaken without that written scope.
